\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कदापि} (kadāpi)}{कदापि (kadāpi)}]{\sk{कदापि} (kadāpi) — ever}

\label{lesson:SA-C93-kadapi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for now, then the Sanskrit for always.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कदापि}}
\textbf{\sk{कदापि}} — \emph{kadāpi} — \textquotedblleft{}ever\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kadāpi} is built from \emph{kadā} \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}, which MW derives from the question stem \emph{ka-}, and the particle \emph{api} \textquotedblleft{}even, also\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}at any time at all\textquotedblright{}. After \emph{na} it turns into \textquotedblleft{}never\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kadāpi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kadāpi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{kadāpi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for now, then the Sanskrit for always, then say \emph{kadāpi} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{कदापि} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Ever\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{विलम्बः} (vilambaḥ)}{विलम्बः (vilambaḥ)}]{\sk{विलम्बः} (vilambaḥ) — a delay}

\label{lesson:SA-C93-vilambah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for always, then the Sanskrit for ever.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{विलम्बः}}
\textbf{\sk{विलम्बः}} — \emph{vilambaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a delay\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vilamba} comes from the verb \emph{vi-√lamb}, the root √lamb \textquotedblleft{}hang\textquotedblright{} with \emph{vi-} \textquotedblleft{}apart, away\textquotedblright{}: to hang back, linger, delay (MW). It lives on as Punjabi \emph{vilamb}, \emph{bilamb} \textquotedblleft{}delay\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11890).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वामः} (vāmaḥ)}{वामः (vāmaḥ)}]{\sk{वामः} (vāmaḥ) — left}

\label{lesson:SA-C93-vamah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for ever, then the Sanskrit for a delay.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वामः}}
\textbf{\sk{वामः}} — \emph{vāmaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}left\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
MW thinks \emph{vāma} \textquotedblleft{}left\textquotedblright{} was perhaps once the same word as \emph{vāma} \textquotedblleft{}lovely, pleasant\textquotedblright{}, from the root √van \textquotedblleft{}love, desire\textquotedblright{}, which would make \textquotedblleft{}the lovely side\textquotedblright{} a polite name for the left; CDIAL keeps the two apart (11533, 11534), so the link is not settled. \emph{vāma} lives on as Hindi \emph{bāyāṁ} \textquotedblleft{}left\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11533).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{दक्षिणः} (dakṣiṇaḥ)}{दक्षिणः (dakṣiṇaḥ)}]{\sk{दक्षिणः} (dakṣiṇaḥ) — right; south}

\label{lesson:SA-C93-daksinah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a delay, then the Sanskrit for left.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दक्षिणः}}
\textbf{\sk{दक्षिणः}} — \emph{dakṣiṇaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}right; south\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dakṣiṇa} is inherited from an Indo-European word for \textquotedblleft{}right\textquotedblright{} that also gave Latin \emph{dexter} (English \emph{dexterous}) and Greek \emph{dexios} (EtymDB). It means \textquotedblleft{}south\textquotedblright{} because someone facing east has the south on the right hand (MW). It lives on as Hindi \emph{dakkhin} \textquotedblleft{}the south\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 6119).
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अन्तः} (antaḥ)}{अन्तः (antaḥ)}]{\sk{अन्तः} (antaḥ) — inside}

\label{lesson:SA-C93-antah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for left, then the Sanskrit for right; south.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अन्तः}}
\textbf{\sk{अन्तः}} — \emph{antaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}inside\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{antaḥ} is \emph{antar} \textquotedblleft{}within, between\textquotedblright{}, with the final \emph{r} said as \emph{ḥ} at the end of a phrase (MW). MW sets it beside Latin \emph{inter} \textquotedblleft{}between\textquotedblright{}, the \emph{inter-} of English \emph{international}, so it is inherited from Indo-European. It lives on as Marathi \emph{āt} \textquotedblleft{}inside\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 356).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}
